transcript.text: In the previous lecture, we had discussion on maximum power transfer theorem for AC circuits and there we saw multiple cases for maximum power transfer when we have AC circuits and now we are going to solve one problem based on one of the cases we saw in the previous lecture. So, let us move on to our problem now. We are required to find the maximum power that can be dissipated in the load. When you observe the network, you will find this is our load which is equal to RL. So our load ZL is purely resistive and this implies XL is equal to 0. The reactive part of the load is equal to 0. Now if you recall, you will find this problem is based on case number 3. In case number 3, the load impedance is purely resistive and for maximum power transfer to the load RL which is our ZL should be equal to the magnitude of thevenin's impedance or we can say ZL which is RL should be equal to under root RTH squared plus XTH squared and the maximum power transferred will be equal to the square of the magnitude of current in thevenin's circuit multiplied to RL and in this problem we are required to find out the maximum power transfer and to calculate Pmax we need magnitude of current i and RL. RL we can have once we have RTH and XTH so to find out RL we need RTH and we need XTH and we know RTH is the real part of ZTH and XTH is the imaginary part of ZTH so we need to find ZTH. Now to find out magnitude of current i we need the magnitude of voltage VTH. So let us move on to the solution and we will first find out voltage VTH and to find out voltage VTH we will make one modification in our network. We will open circuit the load and we will find out the open circuit voltage which is VTH. Now if i connect this point to the ground this point will have the potential VTH. Now to find out VTH i will use nodal analysis. I will consider this to be principal node, this to be reference node and the principal node will have the largest voltage in the network and therefore the two currents in the two branches will leave this node. I will call this current i1 and this current i2 when you apply KCL at this node you will find i1 plus i2 is equal to 0. Now moving on to current i1 it is equal to VTH minus 110 angle 0 degree in volts divided by 6 plus j8 ohms plus current i2. i2 is equal to VTH minus 90 angle 0 degree in volts divided by 6 plus j8 and this should be equal to 0. We can simplify the left hand side as twice of VTH minus 200 angle 0 degree divided by 6 plus j8 and this should be equal to 0. When you multiply both the sides by 6 plus j8 you will have twice of VTH minus 200 angle 0 degree equal to 0. From here we will have VTH VTH will be equal to 100 angle 0 degree in volts. We need the magnitude of VTH and the magnitude of VTH will be 100. So in this way we are done with the calculation of VTH and its magnitude and now we will focus on calculation of ZTH and its magnitude. We will make two changes in our network change number one is open circuiting the load and the change number two is short circuiting the two sources we have and then we will find out impedance ZTH. ZTH is equal to 6 plus j8 ohms in parallel with 6 plus j8 ohms and this should be equal to 6 plus j8 divided by 2 so we have ZTH equal to 3 plus j4 ohms and the real part which is 3 is our RTH and the imaginary part which is 4 is our XTH. Now we will find out the magnitude of ZTH the magnitude of ZTH will be equal to under root 3 squared plus 4 squared so we have 9 plus 16 and therefore ZTH will have the magnitude equal to under root 25 which is 5 and the units will be ohm and for maximum power transfer ZL which is equal to RL should be equal to magnitude of ZTH so this should be equal to RL so we now have RL let's find out magnitude of current i it is equal to magnitude of thevenin voltage VTH divided by magnitude of ZTH plus RL. Magnitude of VTH we know it is 100 magnitude of ZTH plus RL will be equal to under root 8 squared plus 4 squared why because ZTH plus RL will be 3 plus j4 plus 5 real part will get added and the imaginary part is equal to 4 so the magnitude of current i is equal to 100 divided by root 80 and the unit will be amperes. Now moving on to the calculation of maximum power delivered Pmax will be equal to square of this which will be 10 power 4 divided by 80 multiplied to RL which is 5 when you simplify this you will have the maximum power equal to 625 watts this is our answer so i hope this problem is clear to you and you understand how to deal with case number three of maximum power transfer theorem when we have AC circuit
